places.name: Studio Ghibli
places.connection: The primary animation studio where 'The Boy and the Heron' was produced by Hayao Miyazaki and his team over a period of many years.

places.name: Sankeien Garden (Estate Inspiration)
places.connection: A traditional Japanese garden widely believed to be a major inspiration for the lush, sprawling estate and gardens where Mahito moves. Its historic buildings, like the Rinshunkaku villa, and large pond mirror the film's setting.

places.name: Edo-Tokyo Open Air Architectural Museum
places.connection: Located near Studio Ghibli, this museum features relocated historical buildings from the Meiji and Taisho eras. Hayao Miyazaki is a known visitor, and its collection of blended Western-Japanese architecture is a direct parallel to the style of Mahito's new home.

places.name: Meiji Mura (Saigo Tsugumichi Residence)
places.connection: An open-air architectural museum preserving buildings from the Meiji period. The Saigo Tsugumichi Residence, with its mix of Western-style exteriors and Japanese interiors, is cited as a key architectural inspiration for the main house in the film.

places.name: Trinity College Library (The Long Room)
places.connection: The grand, barrel-vaulted ceiling and towering shelves of books in the Long Room bear a striking resemblance to the otherworldly library where Mahito meets his Great-Granduncle. It is considered a strong visual inspiration for the scene.

places.name: Utsunomiya City (Childhood Evacuation Inspiration)
places.connection: The city where Hayao Miyazaki's family evacuated during World War II. This personal history is the direct inspiration for Mahito's story of leaving Tokyo for the countryside after a tragedy. The coordinates are for Utsunomiya Station, a central point in the area.

places.name: Shōsei-en Garden (Kikoku-tei)
places.connection: This tranquil garden, part of the Higashi Honganji Temple, is another cited inspiration for the film's garden aesthetic, with its central pond and surrounding traditional architecture creating an atmosphere similar to Mahito's home.

places.name: Tonogayato Garden
places.connection: A traditional Japanese stroll garden located near Studio Ghibli. Its natural cliff (kokubunji-gaisen), spring-fed pond, and bamboo grove could have served as local inspiration for the varied landscapes on the estate grounds.

places.name: Seisen-ryo at Keep Association (Stone Gate Inspiration)
places.connection: A mountain resort with distinctive rustic stone architecture from the 1930s. Its imposing stone gate and main hall are often suggested as inspirations for the stone structures and entrances seen in the otherworldly tower.

places.name: Ghibli Museum, Mitaka
places.connection: The spiritual home for Ghibli fans worldwide. While not a location from the film, it is a primary pilgrimage destination for admirers of Miyazaki's work and the place to immerse oneself in the Ghibli aesthetic.

places.name: Ghibli Park (Ghibli's Grand Warehouse)
places.connection: A large theme park bringing the world of Studio Ghibli to life. Ghibli's Grand Warehouse, in particular, features architecture and exhibits that evoke the fantastical and nostalgic feelings present in 'The Boy and the Heron.' A major pilgrimage hotspot.

places.name: Shimo-Kitazawa Station Area
places.connection: This neighborhood was home to Genzaburo Yoshino, the author of 'How Do You Live?', the book that inspired the film's title and themes. Fans make pilgrimages here to connect with the literary roots of Miyazaki's movie.

places.name: Roy Thomson Hall
places.connection: The venue for the film's prestigious international premiere on September 7, 2023, where it opened the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF).

places.name: Toho Studios
places.connection: The main studio of Toho Co., Ltd., the Japanese distributor for 'The Boy and the Heron.' An iconic and essential location in the Japanese film industry and the movie's journey to the screen.
